text: June, eighteen ninety-three. A young Indian lawyer is sitting in a first-class compartment on a train in South Africa. He has a valid ticket. A white passenger complains. At Pietermaritzburg station, he is thrown off the train.
He spent that night shivering in the station waiting room, deciding whether to go home or to fight. He stayed, and fought, for more than twenty years.
His name was Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi. When he came home to India in nineteen fifteen, people would come to call him Mahatma, "great soul".
His weapon was satyagraha: holding on to the truth, and resisting without violence.

In nineteen nineteen, in Amritsar, thousands of people gathered peacefully in a walled garden called Jallianwala Bagh. A British general blocked the exit and ordered his troops to fire into the crowd. They fired until they ran out of bullets. The official count was three hundred and seventy-nine dead. Indian estimates were over a thousand.
After Amritsar, millions of Indians who had trusted the British stopped trusting them.
And Gandhi chose the most unlikely weapon in history. Remember that Indian cloth? Remember Manchester? Gandhi told Indians to burn foreign cloth, and spin their own.

He sat at a spinning wheel, the charkha, every day, and wore rough homespun cotton called khadi. The spinning wheel went onto the freedom movement's flag. The cloth that had once made India rich would now help set it free.
In nineteen thirty, he picked an even stranger target: salt. The British taxed it, and Indians were banned from making their own. So Gandhi walked to the sea.
Mr Gandhi, what exactly are you doing?
Then arrest me. And the thousands behind me.
[looking at the crowd, then his notebook] I'll need a bigger notebook.
The Salt March covered about three hundred and eighty kilometres in twenty-four days, and newspapers around the world followed every step.

Not everyone believed in non-violence. Bhagat Singh took up arms, and was hanged at twenty-three. Subhas Chandra Bose raised an army with Japan's help. And Dr B R Ambedkar, born into a so-called untouchable caste, fought for India's most oppressed people.

In the Second World War, about two and a half million Indian soldiers fought for Britain, the largest volunteer army in history. Meanwhile, in nineteen forty-three, a famine in Bengal killed around three million people.
By the end of the war, Britain was broke and exhausted. It could no longer hold on to India.
Freedom was coming. But it was not coming whole.
